Savant

sa-VAHNT -- from French savant, 'knowing,' rooted in Latin sapere, 'to know, be wise.' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Savant is a person of profound and often specialized learning or knowledge.

Even the ship's veteran navigators deferred to the young apprentice, a genuine savant when it came to reading storm patterns in the clouds.

Worked Example

The young savant could name every country's capital and flag by age seven, though he still needed help tying his shoes.

The child's extraordinary, specialized knowledge -- far beyond his years -- is exactly what makes him a savant.

How Savant Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

scholar

scholar: a person with great knowledge in a particular field, especially through formal study

sage

sage: a person known for their wisdom, especially through experience

Antonyms

novice

novice: a person new to and inexperienced in a field

dilettante

dilettante: a person with only a superficial interest or knowledge in something

How Strong Is It? — scholar → sage → savant

scholar vs. savant

scholar vs. savant: By graduate school, she was already considered a promising young scholar in her narrow field.

sage vs. savant

sage vs. savant: Villagers came from three counties away to seek the old sage's advice before the harvest.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — savant (< French savoir)

root — savant (< French savoir): knowing, to know (French, from Latin sapere)

Put it together

Put it together: Savant comes directly from the French word for 'knowing,' itself from Latin sapere, 'to know or be wise' -- English simply borrowed the whole word rather than building it from reusable English pieces.

Use the root in a new word: savoir-faire

Use the root in a new word: savoir-faire: Savoir-faire, literally 'knowing how to do,' is a related French borrowing meaning the ability to act appropriately in any situation.
